passage: Note from Chetan, class teacher. Leela (5) drew hearts all over her page. "I love you, and I love my Nani, and I love mangoes." At snack she gave me half her orange. "It's the good half." Her words run a little ahead of what she means by love, but the orange said something too. I thanked her for both. At pick-up she waved to me until the gate. 😊

qa.q: What did Leela give Chetan at snack?
qa.a: Half her orange.

qa.q: What might Leela feel toward her teacher?
qa.a: Affection, shown by the hearts, her words and sharing the good half. Her words may run ahead of her understanding.

qa.q: How did Chetan respond?
qa.a: He thanked her for both the words and the orange, noticing the small act as well.

qa.q: How might Chetan see her mixing "I love you" with "I love mangoes"?
qa.a: As sincere but not yet precise. The small act of sharing says more than the words.

grounding: Shows a preschooler drawing hearts and saying I love you while sharing a favourite thing.

passage: In a Goan village, Dilnaz, five, ran through the yard to her grandmother Maria, who was shelling peas. "I drew you!" The paper had a huge heart and a round figure in a big hat. "I love you the whole sky." Maria laughed. "The whole sky is big." "And the sea too." Then Dilnaz sat down beside her and shelled peas, dropping most of them on the floor. "I'm helping."

qa.q: What did Dilnaz draw?
qa.a: A huge heart and a round figure in a big hat.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz feel toward Maria?
qa.a: Warm affection, since she runs to her, draws her and then sits down to help.

qa.q: How can Maria respond to both the big words and the help?
qa.a: Welcome both warmly and keep noticing small acts like the helping.

qa.q: How might Maria feel when the peas drop on the floor?
qa.a: Amused and touched, since she is laughing and letting Dilnaz help.

grounding: Shows a young child drawing a heart, saying she loves her grandmother and joining in with a small act.

passage: Every evening in Stockholm, when Oskar came home from work, Kofi met him at the door with a drawing covered in red hearts. “I love you, Papa. This many.” He'd point at every heart. On Saturdays he gave Oskar the last piece of his favourite licorice, even though he loved it. One night Kofi said, “I love you more than the whole sky and all the fish.” Oskar laughed. “That's a lot.” “It's everything,” Kofi said, and fell asleep on his shoulder.

qa.q: What did Kofi give Oskar on Saturdays?
qa.a: The last piece of his favourite licorice.

qa.q: What was Kofi feeling when he said he loved Oskar more than the sky?
qa.a: He felt deep affection and wanted to show it in the biggest words he knew, though his words ran ahead of his understanding.

qa.q: What small acts show Kofi's love?
qa.a: Giving drawings with hearts every evening and sharing his favourite sweet show love through repeated small acts.

qa.q: How might Oskar feel each evening at the door?
qa.a: He likely feels loved and warm, looking forward to Kofi's hearts.

grounding: A preschooler shows love through repeated drawings of hearts, sharing a favourite sweet and big words.

passage: In the hospital waiting room, Gurpreet sat with Disha, the nurse on duty, while her mother had a check-up. She drew a big pink heart, then another, then another, until the page was full. “For Mummy. So she gets better fast.” Disha smiled. “She'll love it.” When her mother came out, Gurpreet ran and pressed the drawing into her hands. “I love you this many!” Her mother knelt and hugged her. “And I love you this many,” she said, and kissed each heart.

qa.q: What colour hearts did Gurpreet draw?
qa.a: Pink.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling as she filled the page with hearts?
qa.a: She felt loving and a bit worried about her mother's check-up, showing care the way she knew how.

qa.q: What did Disha do that supported Gurpreet?
qa.a: Disha stayed with Gurpreet, smiled and assured her that her mother would love the drawing.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's mother feel when she receives the drawing?
qa.a: She'd feel touched and deeply loved, which is why she kisses each heart.

grounding: A preschooler draws hearts for her mother at the hospital, showing love through a small act.

passage: I'm Ujjwal, Irawati's big brother. Irawati says “I love you” to everyone: Mummy, Papa, the milkman, even the stray cat. At first I thought she didn't mean it. But every evening she saves half her sweet for Dadi and takes it to her room. Every morning she gives her doll a kiss before school. I don't know if she knows what love really means yet, but she does something kind every single day.

qa.q: What does Irawati save for Dadi every evening?
qa.a: Half her sweet.

qa.q: What might Irawati be feeling when she says “I love you” to everyone?
qa.a: She probably feels happy and affectionate, and her words may run ahead of full understanding. Ujjwal isn't sure what she understands.

qa.q: What shows Irawati's love more than her words?
qa.a: Her small daily acts, like saving half her sweet for Dadi and kissing her doll.

qa.q: How has Ujjwal's view of Irawati's love changed?
qa.a: He first thought she didn't mean it, but now notices her daily kindnesses.

grounding: A brother observes a preschooler's love shown through repeated small acts more than through her many I love yous.

passage:
Monday: Nandini drew a page of wobbly red hearts and pushed it under Grandma Elizabeth's door. "I love you a hundred!" she shouted, then ran off.

Thursday: Grandma Elizabeth had a cold. Nandini dragged in her favourite blanket, the one with ducks, and spread it over Grandma's knees. "You can keep it till you're better. Maybe till lunch."

Sunday: Nandini said "I love you" to Grandma, to the cat and to a pancake. Grandma laughed. The duck blanket, though, was still on Grandma's chair, folded by small hands.

qa.q: What did Nandini push under Grandma Elizabeth's door on Monday?
qa.a: A page of wobbly red hearts.

qa.q: Why might Nandini have offered the blanket only "till lunch"?
qa.a: She cared about Grandma and wanted her to feel better, but she also loved that blanket, so she probably felt a little torn about giving it up.

qa.q: How could Grandma Elizabeth show Nandini that her small acts count?
qa.a: She could thank her for something specific, such as "your ducks kept me warm", so Nandini learns her caring actions matter as much as the words.

qa.q: How might Grandma Elizabeth see Nandini saying "I love you" to a pancake?
qa.a: She finds it funny and can see Nandini is still learning what the word means, while the folded blanket shows the love more clearly 🙂

grounding: It shows a young child expressing love through drawings, words and sharing a favourite thing, with the words running ahead of their meaning.
